title: FeasibilityEphemerisComputed
description:
feasibility-service has propagated ONE satellite over ONE horizon bucket and is publishing where it was, as sampled positions on the WGS84 ellipsoid. This is the orbit itself, not a consequence of it: unlike feasibility.opportunities.computed.v1, nothing here depends on a customer request, and the sweep that produces it runs on a timer rather than on a message.

It exists because the read model held no ephemeris and therefore no satellite path. Interpolating a curve through committed footprint centroids would have drawn something that looks like an orbit and is not one, which is worse than an absent layer because a viewer would believe it.

One satellite per event, not the whole constellation. A twelve-satellite bundle would be twelve times the payload for a consumer that renders one satellite's plan at a time, and a single oversized message is also a single message to redeliver.

event_id.description: DERIVED, not random, for this event type. The producing sweep is a timer rather than a message handler, so it has no upstream event_id to inherit deduplication from — it computes a UUIDv5 over (satellite_id, horizon start, tle_epoch) instead. Re-running the sweep over a bucket it has already covered therefore collides on the outbox's unique event_id and inserts nothing, which is what makes a rolling sweep safe to run every few minutes.

correlation_id.description: The sweep's own correlation id. There is no customer transaction to correlate to — this event is caused by the passage of time, not by a request.

causation_id.description: Null, always. The envelope permits null for events with no antecedent, and a timer tick is not an event anybody published.

horizon.description: The half-open bucket these samples cover. Buckets are aligned to a fixed grid so that the same bucket is always the same interval — which is what lets the derived event_id above be stable across sweeps, and what stops two sweeps producing overlapping-but-different tracks.

tle_reference.description: The element set this track was propagated from. Singular, because one event is one satellite. This is what makes a drawn orbit auditable: a track that disagrees with reality is a question about which TLE produced it, and without this it is unanswerable.

epoch.description: Time origin for the sample offsets. Normally equal to horizon.start and carried separately anyway, because the samples are meaningless without it and a consumer must never have to infer it.

sample_interval_s.description: Nominal spacing between samples. Descriptive, not authoritative: every sample carries its own offset, so a consumer reconstructs times from the offsets and uses this only to reason about resolution. Stating the interval AND the per-sample offset is deliberate redundancy — deriving times from the interval alone would let one dropped sample silently shift the rest of the track.

sample_count.description: Length of the samples array. Redundant on purpose, like opportunity_count: consumers log and alert on track size without deserialising it. Two is the minimum because one point is a position, not a path.

prefixItems.description: Seconds after `epoch`. An offset rather than an RFC 3339 timestamp: a full timestamp per sample is more bytes than the position it labels, and this is the one event whose size is dominated by repetition.
Longitude, decimal degrees, WGS84. FIRST, as everywhere else in this system.

Height above the WGS84 ellipsoid, metres. Not above terrain, and not a slant range. Unbounded here rather than clamped to a LEO band, because the contract should not decide what orbits this system may carry.

items.description:
One sample: [seconds_after_epoch, longitude_deg, latitude_deg, altitude_m].

A positional tuple rather than an object, because at this cardinality the field names would be most of the payload. The cost is the documented generator gap — neither binding renders prefixItems, so both see a bare list of numbers and the per-element bounds above are asserted by the schema at the boundary rather than by the type. `items` restates 'every element is a number', which prefixItems plus maxItems already implies, purely so the generators emit a numeric slice instead of an untyped one.
